headline: NRC Changes Withholding and Comment Procedures
dek: The direct final rule also aligns advisory-committee terminology and codifies security-eligibility criteria; it takes effect Oct. 26 unless significant adverse comments prompt withdrawal.

sources.title: NRC Modernization; Rulemaking Procedure, Federal Advisory Committee Act Alignment, Access, and Security Eligibility

lead.creator: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary meeting photograph is licensed CC BY 2.0 on Wikimedia Commons and traces to the NRC's official Flickr account.
lead.attribution: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, CC BY 2.0
lead.caption: NRC staff brief the Commission about public participation and agency requirements in 2013. The archival scene illustrates the procedures addressed by the agency's 2026 rule.
lead.alt: Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff seated at a public briefing table in a meeting room.

charts.caption: The rule addresses proprietary-information affidavits, post-promulgation comments, advisory committees and security-eligibility criteria.
charts.alt: Graphic lists four procedural areas changed by the NRC rule.

charts.caption: The rule is scheduled for Oct. 26, 2026, but significant adverse comments received by Sept. 10 could cause the NRC to withdraw it.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Sept. 10 comment deadline and Oct. 26 scheduled effective date.

paragraphs: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission has issued a direct final rule changing several internal and public-facing procedures, including how proprietary-information requests are supported and how the agency handles comments submitted after a rule is published.

The rule is scheduled to take effect Oct. 26, 2026. Because the NRC used a direct-final process, it says it will withdraw the rule if it receives significant adverse comments by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on Sept. 10.

One change removes a requirement that an affidavit seeking to withhold proprietary information describe the harm disclosure would cause. Other withholding requirements remain, and the change does not make every confidentiality request automatic.

The NRC also revises or removes its self-imposed procedure for post-promulgation comments in 10 CFR 2.804. The agency characterizes that process as duplicative of other petition and rulemaking mechanisms; the rule does not end ordinary notice-and-comment requirements that otherwise apply.
Advisory-committee terminology, charters, appointments and reporting are being aligned with General Services Administration rules issued in December 2025 under the Federal Advisory Committee Act.

A fourth part codifies national-security eligibility criteria from Security Executive Agent Directive 4 that the NRC says it already uses internally. Codification places those criteria in the agency's regulations rather than creating a new eligibility system.
The NRC says the package imposes no new obligations or costs on licensees or the public. That is the agency's regulatory assessment, not an independently measured outcome after implementation.

Direct-final status is important: the published text is a completed agency action, but its Oct. 26 start remains conditional during the adverse-comment window. A withdrawal or companion proposal would appear in a later public record.
facts: Comments capable of triggering withdrawal are due Sept. 10, 2026.
The scheduled effective date is Oct. 26, 2026.
The rule changes four procedural areas.
The NRC says it creates no new external obligations or costs.
uncertainty: The rule can be withdrawn if the NRC receives significant adverse comments.
The agency's no-cost conclusion has not yet been tested through implementation.
seoTitle: NRC changes rulemaking and withholding procedures in 2026
seoDescription: The NRC's direct final rule changes withholding affidavits, post-publication comments, advisory committees and security criteria, subject to a Sept. 10 comment gate.

headline: OCC, FDIC Propose New CRA Bank Size Thresholds
dek: The plan would classify most supervised banks as small while leaving institutions holding most assets in the large-bank category.
entities: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

sources.title: Community Reinvestment Act Regulations
sources.publisher: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation

lead.creator: Aurora30
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer dedicated the bank-branch photograph to the public domain on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A First Citizens Bank branch in Beaufort, South Carolina, in an archival photograph. The OCC-FDIC proposal would apply size-based CRA tests to supervised banks, not decide the rating of this branch or institution.
lead.alt: Brick bank branch with columns and a drive-through under a blue sky.

charts.caption: The proposal would set small-bank status below $1 billion, intermediate status from $1 billion through $10 billion, and large-bank status above $10 billion.
charts.alt: Graphic compares proposed one-billion and ten-billion-dollar CRA thresholds.

charts.caption: Using 2024–25 data, the agencies estimate 79.8% of their 3,577 supervised banks would be small but would hold 4.9% of assets.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 79.8 percent of banks and 4.9 percent of assets in the proposed small category.

paragraphs: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation are proposing new Community Reinvestment Act size categories: small banks below $1 billion in assets, intermediate banks from $1 billion through $10 billion, and large banks above $10 billion.
The proposal is on Federal Register public inspection ahead of scheduled Aug. 12 publication. Its 60-day comment period begins with publication; the thresholds are not currently in force.

Existing thresholds are below $412 million for small banks, $412 million through $1.649 billion for intermediate institutions and more than $1.649 billion for large banks. Those figures remain the relevant comparison until a final rule changes them.
The agencies estimate that 79.8% of the 3,577 banks they supervised in the 2024–25 data would fall in the proposed small category. Those institutions represented 4.9% of supervised-bank assets.
Small and intermediate banks together would hold an estimated 14.6% of assets. The figures show why the share of institutions and the share of assets can point in different directions.

Banks with $10 billion or less in assets would face fewer data-reporting duties, and lending tests would focus on major retail product lines under the proposal. Public files could be maintained online rather than only at physical locations.

The plan comes from the OCC and FDIC and therefore does not by itself set rules for every bank overseen by the Federal Reserve. It also does not resolve litigation that has enjoined the agencies' 2023 CRA rule.

No lending result follows automatically from a size label. The public record invites comment on supervisory design; any final thresholds, compliance dates and effects would require a later final rule and implementation.
facts: Proposed thresholds are below $1 billion, $1 billion through $10 billion, and above $10 billion.
The agencies estimate 79.8% of 3,577 supervised banks would be small.
Those proposed small banks held an estimated 4.9% of supervised assets.
A 60-day comment period is expected after publication.
uncertainty: This is a proposal, not a final rule.
The agencies' distribution estimates do not predict lending outcomes and do not cover every U.S. bank regulator.
seoTitle: OCC, FDIC propose $1B and $10B CRA bank thresholds
seoDescription: A 2026 CRA proposal would call banks under $1 billion small and those above $10 billion large, changing testing and data duties for OCC- and FDIC-supervised institutions.

headline: NIST Seeks Guardrails for AI in Vulnerability Database
dek: The 60-day inquiry seeks evidence on automation, human review, auditability and safeguards for the federal vulnerability database.
entities: National Institute of Standards and Technology

sources.title: Request for Information: Modernizing the National Vulnerability Database in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

sources.title: National Vulnerability Database
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology

lead.creator: Maj. Christopher Vasquez / U.S. Air Force
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary photograph was made by a U.S. Air Force employee in an official capacity and is a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.attribution: Maj. Christopher Vasquez / U.S. Air Force, public domain
lead.caption: Cybersecurity personnel work at Port San Antonio in a U.S. Air Force photograph. The scene is illustrative and does not depict NVD analysts or a specific vulnerability.
lead.alt: Cybersecurity workers seated at computer stations in a dark operations room.

charts.caption: NIST asks about seven areas spanning vulnerability management, dissemination, prioritization, remediation, data, development and the NVD's long-term vision.
charts.alt: Graphic lists seven areas in NIST's NVD modernization inquiry.

charts.caption: NVD automation can ingest a CVE record in about one hour before analysts add severity and product-version context.
charts.alt: Graphic shows automated CVE intake followed by analyst enrichment and published data.

paragraphs: The National Institute of Standards and Technology is asking cybersecurity practitioners how artificial intelligence could help modernize the National Vulnerability Database without sacrificing human review, auditability or trust.

The request for information is on public inspection for Aug. 12 publication and a 60-day response window. It is a question-gathering exercise, not a decision to let an AI system classify or remediate vulnerabilities.

The NVD automatically ingests Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures records in about an hour, according to NIST. Analysts then enrich records with severity scores, affected product versions and other context used by security tools.

NIST organized its questions around seven areas: vulnerability-management processes, information dissemination, prioritization, remediation, data and standards, software-development practices, and a five-year vision for the NVD.
The agency specifically asks which steps are suitable for automation, where human review must remain, and how AI-assisted decisions could be audited and explained.
It also seeks safeguards against incorrect remediation advice. That concern matters because a plausible but wrong recommendation can disrupt a system or leave a real flaw unresolved.

NIST says CVE volume rose 263% from 2020 through 2025. Nearly 42,000 records were enriched in 2025, 45% more than the prior year, while submissions in the first quarter of 2026 were nearly one-third higher than a year earlier.

Those growth figures explain the scaling problem but do not prove that any particular AI architecture will solve it. NIST has not selected a model, vendor or automated remediation design, and later action will depend on the evidence it receives.
facts: NVD automated intake takes about one hour before analyst enrichment.
The RFI covers seven modernization areas.
NIST says CVE volume rose 263% from 2020 through 2025.
Nearly 42,000 records were enriched in 2025.
uncertainty: The RFI does not commit NIST to a particular AI system or architecture.
Agency workload growth does not establish that automation will be accurate or safe without validation.
seoTitle: NIST seeks input on AI modernization of the NVD
seoDescription: NIST's 2026 inquiry asks where AI can assist the National Vulnerability Database while preserving human review, auditability and safeguards against wrong remediation.

headline: National Parks Require Local Approval for E-Scooters
dek: A final rule creates a separate category for powered micromobility devices, with park-by-park designations and wilderness restrictions.

lead.creator: Thomson200
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary National Mall photograph was released under CC0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A shared electric scooter stands on the National Mall in 2019. Under the new rule, powered micromobility remains prohibited in a park unless its superintendent designates where it may operate.
lead.alt: Green electric scooter parked beside a walkway on the National Mall in Washington.

charts.caption: The default remains prohibited; a superintendent can designate certain roads, parking areas, improved paths or sidewalks for use.
charts.alt: Graphic shows powered micromobility prohibited by default and allowed only on designated surfaces.

charts.caption: The category covers devices such as e-scooters, hoverboards and Segways up to 150 pounds, while e-bikes and accessibility devices follow separate rules.
charts.alt: Graphic lists examples and exclusions in the National Park Service micromobility rule.

paragraphs: Powered micromobility devices such as e-scooters, hoverboards and Segways will remain prohibited by default in National Park Service areas unless a superintendent affirmatively designates places where they may be used.

The final rule is on Federal Register public inspection for Aug. 12 publication and is scheduled to take effect 30 days after publication. It creates a regulatory category distinct from motor vehicles, bicycles, e-bikes and human-powered coasting devices.

Covered devices have no combustion engine and can weigh up to 150 pounds. E-bikes are governed separately, and wheelchairs or other mobility aids used by people with disabilities are not folded into the same restrictions.

A superintendent can designate roads, parking areas, paved or gravel paths, sidewalks and other improved surfaces through a public compendium notice. Opening terrain that has never been improved requires formal rulemaking.
Possession in statutory wilderness remains prohibited unless another law permits it. A designation elsewhere in a park does not override that wilderness restriction.

Superintendents may set limits on speed, dimensions, weight, device type, parking, time or season. State and local helmet, age, licensing and speed rules also apply unless federal law supersedes them.

The Park Service received 63 comments and says it made no substantive change from the proposal. It cited an industry estimate of 84.9 million shared e-scooter trips in North America in 2024 as context for the rule.

Visitors still need to check the current compendium and alerts for the specific park they plan to enter. The national rule supplies a framework; it is not blanket permission to ride an e-scooter in every park.
facts: Powered micromobility is prohibited by default in National Park Service areas.
Superintendents may designate certain improved surfaces.
The category includes non-combustion devices up to 150 pounds.
E-bikes and accessibility devices are governed separately.
uncertainty: Individual park designations and restrictions can differ and change.
The effective date depends on final Federal Register publication.
seoTitle: National Park e-scooter rule keeps park-by-park permissions
seoDescription: The 2026 National Park Service rule keeps e-scooters prohibited by default and lets superintendents designate specific improved surfaces for powered micromobility.

headline: NSF Offers Up to $40 Million for Secure Open Source
dek: PESOSE proposals are due Sept. 1, with three tracks supporting planning, ecosystem growth and security or privacy work.

sources.title: Pathways to Enable Secure Open-Source Ecosystems (PESOSE)

lead.creator: Auregann
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary university open-source workshop photograph is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: Participants work at a 2025 Wikimedia hackathon workshop at Palermo University. The archival scene illustrates collaborative open-source work and does not depict a PESOSE award or applicant.
lead.alt: Adults working together at laptops around tables during a university hackathon workshop.

charts.caption: Track 1 supports planning up to $300,000; Tracks 2 and 3 support ecosystem growth or security and privacy work up to $1.5 million.
charts.alt: Graphic compares three PESOSE tracks and maximum award sizes.

charts.caption: A proposal-preparation webinar is scheduled Aug. 12, and the first full-proposal deadline is Sept. 1 at 5 p.m. submitter local time.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Aug. 12 webinar and Sept. 1 proposal deadline.

paragraphs: The National Science Foundation is making up to $40 million available through a new program for building secure, sustainable open-source software ecosystems, with the first full proposals due Sept. 1.
NSF's Pathways to Enable Secure Open-Source Ecosystems program, or PESOSE, has three tracks. A proposal-preparation webinar is scheduled online for Aug. 12 from 1 to 2 p.m. Eastern.
Track 1 offers planning awards of up to $300,000. NSF estimates about 30 awards in that track, aimed at governance, community design and preparation for larger ecosystem work.

Tracks 2 and 3 offer awards of up to $1.5 million. Track 2 is for establishing or expanding an ecosystem, while Track 3 focuses on safety, security and privacy improvements; NSF estimates roughly 10 awards in each.

Eligible lead organizations include accredited U.S. two- and four-year institutions and certain U.S. nonprofit organizations. The solicitation requires an existing, publicly available open-source software project rather than a plan to open a wholly private product later.
Each proposal has one lead organization, though subawards are allowed. Track 1 and Track 2 awardees must participate in the NSF I-Corps program, and voluntary committed cost sharing is not allowed.

The Sept. 1 deadline is 5 p.m. in the submitting organization's local time. NSF lists a second target date of March 2, 2027, which gives prospective teams another cycle but does not extend the September round.
The award counts and $40 million total are estimates contingent on proposals, review and available funds. Meeting the eligibility rules or joining the webinar does not guarantee an award.
facts: NSF says up to $40 million may be available.
Track 1 awards are capped at $300,000.
Track 2 and 3 awards are capped at $1.5 million.
The first proposal deadline is Sept. 1, 2026 at 5 p.m. submitter local time.
uncertainty: Funding and award counts are estimates, not awards already made.
Eligibility depends on the full solicitation and does not guarantee selection.
seoTitle: NSF PESOSE open-source grants: tracks and Sept. 1 deadline
seoDescription: NSF's PESOSE program offers up to $40 million across planning, ecosystem and security tracks for existing public open-source projects.

headline: FDA Updates Fresh-Cut Produce Safety Guide
dek: The final nonbinding guide adds antimicrobial, supply-chain and time-temperature examples while clarifying which ready-to-eat produce it covers.

sources.title: Guidance: Guide To Minimize Biological Hazards in Ready-To-Eat Fresh-Cut Produce

lead.creator: U.S. Department of Agriculture
lead.rightsBasis: The documentary produce-packing photograph was made by a USDA employee in an official capacity and is a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.attribution: U.S. Department of Agriculture, public domain
lead.caption: Just-picked zucchini waits beside a processing trailer at a Virginia farm in a 2013 USDA photograph. The archival scene is illustrative; FDA's 2026 guidance is for manufacturers and processors of covered ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce.
lead.alt: Basket of freshly harvested green zucchini in a field with a processing trailer and tractor behind it.

charts.caption: The guide covers ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce that is not low-moisture food, clarified as water activity above 0.85.
charts.alt: Graphic shows ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce and a water-activity threshold above 0.85.

charts.caption: The final guide adds an antimicrobial process-control example, more pathogen supply-chain examples and added time-temperature recommendations.
charts.alt: Graphic lists three updates in FDA's 2026 fresh-cut produce guidance.

paragraphs: The Food and Drug Administration has finalized updated safety guidance for manufacturers and processors of ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce, replacing a 2008 guide and completing a draft first issued in 2018.

The notice is on Federal Register public inspection for Aug. 12 publication. It is industry guidance reflecting FDA's current thinking, not a recall, an outbreak alert or a declaration that a particular product is unsafe.
The guide covers ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce that is not a low-moisture food. FDA clarified that boundary as food with water activity greater than 0.85.

Its purpose is to help facilities apply current good manufacturing practices and hazard-analysis and risk-based preventive controls under 21 CFR part 117. Companies may use alternative approaches if they satisfy applicable statutes and regulations.
Compared with the draft, the final guide adds another example of an antimicrobial treatment used as a process control. It also expands examples of supply-chain programs for pathogen hazards.

FDA added time-and-temperature recommendations addressing conditions that can allow microorganisms to grow. The document's examples must be read in the context of a facility's ingredients, process and hazard analysis.

The guidance does not impose a new mandatory approval process for every bag of cut produce. Binding requirements come from the underlying law and regulations, while the guide explains one way industry can meet them.

Consumers should not infer that all fresh-cut produce carries the same risk or that the notice changes personal medical guidance. The immediate audience is the businesses that manufacture and process covered food.
facts: The final guide supersedes FDA's 2008 fresh-cut produce guidance.
It finalizes a draft issued in 2018.
Covered food has water activity above 0.85 and is ready-to-eat fresh-cut produce.
The guide adds antimicrobial, supply-chain and time-temperature examples.
uncertainty: The guidance is nonbinding and allows lawful alternative approaches.
The notice does not identify an unsafe product or establish consumer-level risk for every fresh-cut item.
seoTitle: FDA finalizes 2026 fresh-cut produce safety guidance
seoDescription: FDA's updated nonbinding guide for fresh-cut produce processors adds antimicrobial, pathogen supply-chain and time-temperature examples and clarifies scope.
